narrative:
The model predicted a 77% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Three factors drove this outcome, ranked by importance. Your class rank at the end of your third year was the strongest influence; being in the bottom decile (compared to an average of roughly the sixth decile among accepted students) strongly pushed the prediction toward failure. Next, your LSAT score of 24 was well below the 37-point average of accepted applicants and added further weight toward a likely bar exam failure. Finally, your first-year class rank, also in the bottom decile against an average around the sixth decile, reinforced the same negative direction.

Taken together, these academic performance signals led the model to conclude that the risk of failing the bar was too high for admission. Family income, undergraduate GPA, and full-time work plans played only minor roles and did not change the outcome.

You should focus on raising your academic performance and retaking the LSAT to reach at least the mid-30s. Once you can demonstrate stronger grades and test scores, reapply; the model will then see a much higher likelihood of passing the bar and is likely to support admission.
